lessons.title: The solar constant
lessons.goal: Understand how much sunlight reaches a directly facing surface outside the atmosphere.

segments.title: A power for every square metre
segments.text: Imagine placing a flat detector just outside Earth's atmosphere, facing the Sun directly. The solar constant describes the radiant power arriving at each square metre of that detector, at Earth's mean distance from the Sun. A value of 1360 watts per square metre means that each square metre receives 1360 joules of radiant energy every second. It is an intensity: power divided by area. It is not the temperature of sunlight, and it is not the total power emitted by the Sun. Begin with that physical picture before trying to remember a definition. Ask yourself what is arriving, where it is measured, and which way the receiving surface faces.

segments.title: Location and orientation matter
segments.text: The definition includes two conditions. First, the detector is outside the atmosphere. Clouds and atmospheric gases have not yet reflected or absorbed the incoming radiation. The intensity measured at the ground can therefore differ from the solar constant. Second, the receiving surface is perpendicular to the incoming rays. Tilting the same detector spreads a beam across a different effective area. When the Sun is directly overhead, a horizontal surface faces the rays directly. A question about that location is not asking for the average over the whole Earth. Circle the words that specify the location and orientation before choosing a calculation. These small details tell you which model is appropriate.

segments.title: Turn an intensity into a power
segments.text: To calculate the power arriving on a directly facing detector, multiply the intensity by its area. A detector with an area of half a square metre receives half the power that arrives at one square metre. At 1360 watts per square metre, it receives 680 watts. Notice the units: watts per square metre multiplied by square metres gives watts. If a question then asks for energy received in ten seconds, multiply that power by ten seconds. Do not add this extra step when the question only asks for power. Keep intensity, power and energy separate by writing a quantity name beside each number before substituting values.

segments.title: Build the exam answer
segments.text: For a definition, give a compact statement that contains the quantity and the conditions: radiant power received per unit area, outside the atmosphere at Earth's mean distance from the Sun, on a surface perpendicular to the rays. A numerical value alone does not define the quantity. In a calculation, first decide whether the value provided is a directly facing intensity or an already averaged intensity. You will meet a factor of four in the next lesson, but it does not belong automatically in every solar calculation. Before continuing, try saying the definition without looking. Then explain why a measurement under a cloud at midday would not directly measure the solar constant.

bridge.title: Energy, power and intensity
bridge.text: Energy is the amount transferred, measured in joules (J). Power is the energy transferred each second: 1 watt (W) means 1 joule per second. Intensity is the power reaching each square metre. W m⁻² means watts per square metre.

blocks.title: Sunlight brings energy
paragraphs: Sunlight carries energy through space as radiation: energy travelling in electromagnetic waves. These waves can travel through empty space. Imagine a flat detector just outside Earth’s atmosphere, facing the Sun directly. Sunlight transfers energy to it every second.

The solar constant, written S, tells us the power arriving at each square metre of that surface at Earth’s average distance from the Sun. A value of 1360 W m⁻² means that every square metre receives 1360 joules each second. This is an intensity, or power divided by area.
A larger detector collects more power because it catches more of the beam. The intensity can stay the same across both a small detector and a large one.
blocks.key: Intensity tells us how much power arrives per square metre. It does not tell us the Sun’s total power or the temperature of the detector.

blocks.title: Where and how we measure it
paragraphs: Earth’s atmosphere is the layer of gases around the planet. Clouds and gases reflect or absorb some sunlight. Reflection sends radiation away; absorption transfers its energy to matter. A measurement at the ground has already been affected by these processes. The solar constant refers to sunlight before it enters the atmosphere.

The detector must also face the rays directly. Its surface is perpendicular to them, meaning that the rays meet it at a right angle of 90°. If the detector tilts, the same beam spreads across a larger patch of surface. Less power then arrives at each square metre of that patch.
In the diagram, the dashed line marks a measurement position outside the atmosphere. The arrows below it show some of the different paths sunlight can take.

blocks.title: From each square metre to a whole detector
paragraphs: Suppose the intensity is 1360 W m⁻² and the detector’s directly facing area is 0.50 m². It collects half the power received by one square metre: 680 W. In P = SA, P is the received power, S is the solar intensity and A is the directly facing area.

Power is a rate: 680 W means 680 joules arrive every second. Over 10 seconds, the energy received is 6800 J. In E = Pt, E is energy and t is the time in seconds. This assumes the power stays constant during that time.
The three quantities describe different things: intensity concerns each square metre, power concerns the whole detector, and energy adds up what arrives over a period of time.

blocks.title: Why the distance is part of the definition
paragraphs: The word “constant” gives us a useful reference value. It does not mean that sunlight has exactly the same intensity everywhere in space. At a greater distance from the Sun, its radiation is spread over a larger area and the intensity is smaller.

Earth’s distance from the Sun varies during its orbit, so the definition uses its mean distance. Mean means average. The Sun’s output also varies slightly. Using a reference value lets us compare surfaces under the same incoming sunlight.
The solar constant describes a directly facing surface. It is different from the average sunlight received over the whole planet, including the night side. That whole-planet average is the next idea.
blocks.key: The solar constant is power per unit area, outside the atmosphere, at Earth’s mean distance from the Sun, on a surface perpendicular to the rays.

checkpoint.prompt: Two directly facing detectors have areas of 1 m² and 2 m². They are side by side outside the atmosphere. How do the intensity and received power compare?
checkpoint.answer: They receive the same intensity because the sunlight per square metre is the same. The 2 m² detector receives twice the power because its area is twice as large.

lessons.title: Radiation across a planet
lessons.goal: Understand why the sunlight averaged over a whole spherical planet is S/4.

segments.title: The shadow tells you what is intercepted
segments.text: Parallel rays from a distant star reach a spherical planet. From the star's direction, the planet blocks a circular disc, not its entire curved surface. If the planet has radius R, that projected disc has area pi R squared. Multiply the solar intensity by this area to obtain the total incident power. This is the same reasoning as using the area of a detector, but now the area must face the beam. The back of the planet does not intercept additional sunlight. It contributes to the planet's total surface area, but not to the cross-section catching the incoming beam. Trace the beam in the diagram and identify these two different areas.

It contributes to the planet's total surface area, but not to the cross-section catching the incoming beam. Trace the beam in the diagram and identify these two different areas.

segments.title: Spread that power over the whole sphere
segments.text: To find the global mean incident intensity, divide the intercepted power by the total area of the spherical surface. The intercepted power is S times pi R squared. The total surface area is four pi R squared. Dividing cancels both pi and R squared, leaving S divided by four. A solar constant of 1360 watts per square metre therefore corresponds to a global mean incident intensity of 340 watts per square metre. The radius disappears because both areas scale with its square. This result is a geometrical average. It does not say that every location on the planet receives 340 watts per square metre at every moment.

checkpoint.prompt: Pause and explain
checkpoint.text: Derive S/4 from projected and spherical areas.
checkpoint.answer: Sunlight is intercepted over πR². Averaging is over the whole 4πR² surface. The area ratio is 1/4. 1400/4 = 350 W m⁻².

segments.title: A local value answers a different question
segments.text: At a location where the Sun is directly overhead, a directly facing surface receives the full local incident intensity before reflection or absorption. At an oblique angle, a given beam is spread over a larger surface area. At night, direct sunlight is absent. A global average combines illumination across locations and time into a simple model. This distinction is why you must read whether the question describes a small region, a detector, an entire planet or an already averaged intensity. If the problem already states that 340 watts per square metre is the global mean, dividing it by four again counts the averaging twice. Always write what the given value represents.

segments.title: Explain the geometry in words and symbols
segments.text: An exam question may ask you to explain the factor of four instead of simply calculate an average. Name both areas and show their ratio. Sunlight is intercepted over the circular cross-section, pi R squared, but the global average is taken over the spherical surface, four pi R squared. The ratio is one quarter. Avoid saying only that half the Earth is dark: day and night alone do not explain the complete factor of four, because illumination is also oblique over most of the day side. Finally, keep averaging separate from absorption. We have calculated incident intensity; in the next lesson albedo determines the fraction that is reflected.

worked.title: Explain the ratio 1400/350
worked.prompt: The solar intensity at Earth is approximately 1400 W m⁻². Suggest why the average received per unit area of Earth is 350 W m⁻².

bridge.title: A flat circle and a sphere
bridge.text: A disc is a filled, flat circle. Its area is πR², where R is the radius: the distance from the centre to the edge. A sphere is a ball-shaped object. Its total curved surface area is 4πR². Area is measured in square metres (m²); it is not volume.

blocks.title: The circular area that catches sunlight
paragraphs: Rays from a distant star reach a planet in almost parallel lines. Parallel lines travel in the same direction without spreading apart. Seen from the star, the planet covers a circle. This circle shows how much of the beam the planet intercepts, meaning catches or blocks.

The light actually strikes the curved day side. The flat circle is a way to measure its projected area: the area seen when looking along the incoming rays. It has the same radius R as the planet and area πR².
At a solar intensity S, the total incoming power is SπR². Rays outside the circle miss the planet. The top and bottom rays in the diagram mark the edges of the beam caught by the planet.

blocks.title: Averaging over the whole surface
paragraphs: A global mean is an average over the whole planet. We find the mean incoming intensity by dividing the total incoming power by the entire surface area, including the night side.

The planet catches sunlight over an area πR², but its whole surface has area 4πR². Dividing SπR² by 4πR² leaves S/4. The factors π and R² cancel because they multiply both the top and the bottom of the fraction.

For S = 1360 W m⁻², the global mean is 340 W m⁻². Averaging is a calculation: it does not mean that sunlight physically spreads evenly around the planet or that the night side receives direct sunlight.

equations.label: The area ratio gives the average
lines: The common π and R² factors cancel: I̅_in = S / 4

blocks.title: Why sunlight is weaker on a sloping surface
paragraphs: Local intensity means the intensity at one place. Where the Sun is overhead, a horizontal surface faces the rays directly. Closer to sunrise or sunset, the rays meet the ground at a slant. The same beam then covers a larger area, so less power arrives per square metre.

To describe the angle, we use the normal: an imaginary line at right angles to the surface. The symbol θ, called theta, is the angle between the incoming ray direction and this normal. For a small surface patch, I = S cos θ. Here I is the local intensity and cos θ is the geometrical factor that accounts for the tilt.
At θ = 60°, the beam covers twice the directly facing area, so I = S/2. At night there is no direct sunlight. These local values are different from the average over the whole sphere.
blocks.key: Local intensity varies from place to place. The global mean combines those different values into one average.

blocks.title: Why the factor is four, not two
paragraphs: Day and night explain part of the reduction in average sunlight, but not all of it. Even on the day side, most of the curved surface meets the rays at a slant. These places receive less power per square metre than a surface facing the Sun directly.

Both effects are already included in the area ratio πR² / 4πR². We do not need a separate correction for night-time after taking this ratio. A larger planet catches more total power, but its surface area increases by the same factor, so its global mean is still S/4 at the same solar intensity.
So far this is incoming radiation, also called incident radiation. Some will be reflected. The next lesson explains how to find the fraction that is absorbed.
blocks.key: The factor of four comes from the circular catching area divided by the whole spherical surface area.

checkpoint.answer: Sunlight also strikes much of the day side at a slant, spreading the beam across a larger area. The catching area πR² divided by the whole surface area 4πR² accounts for both effects and gives S/4.

segments.title: Follow what happens to incoming radiation
segments.text: When radiation reaches a surface or a planet, some can be scattered or reflected away. Albedo is the fraction of the total incident power that is scattered back out of the system being considered. An albedo of zero point three means that thirty percent of the incident power is reflected. It does not mean that thirty percent is absorbed. Because albedo is a ratio of two powers, the units cancel. It has no unit. You can express it as a decimal fraction or a percentage, provided you make that choice clear. In an equation, use the decimal fraction: zero point three rather than thirty when the albedo is thirty percent.

segments.title: Find the absorbed fraction

The reflected intensity is 102 watts per square metre. Together they recover the incident 340. That check is useful because it catches reversed fractions. blocks.title: The fraction reflected
paragraphs: When sunlight reaches a surface, some is reflected away. Albedo is the fraction of the incoming power that is reflected. We use the symbol α, called alpha. An albedo of 0.30 means that 30% of the incoming power is reflected.

Albedo is found by dividing reflected power by incoming power. Both quantities have the same unit, so their units cancel. This makes albedo dimensionless, meaning it has no unit. An albedo of 0 means no incoming power is reflected; an albedo of 1 means all of it is reflected.
For a whole planet, the reflected light includes sunlight sent back towards space by the surface, clouds and atmosphere. In an equation, 30% is written as the fraction 0.30.

equations.label: Compare the reflected part with the incoming whole

blocks.title: Adding up the incoming radiation
paragraphs: Imagine a surface where incoming radiation can only be reflected or absorbed. If 100 W m⁻² is reflected and 400 W m⁻² is absorbed, then 500 W m⁻² must have arrived. The two parts account for the whole incoming amount.

The reflected fraction is therefore 100/500 = 0.20. Dividing 100 by 400 would compare the reflected part with the absorbed part. It would not compare reflection with the whole incoming amount, so it would not give albedo.

This two-part description assumes no transmission. Transmission means radiation passing through a material. If some passes through, it is a third part of the incoming energy and must be included in the total.

equations.label: A surface with reflection and absorption only

blocks.title: The fraction absorbed
paragraphs: If reflection and absorption are the only possibilities, their fractions add to one. When the reflected fraction is α, the absorbed fraction is 1 − α. For an albedo of 0.30, the absorbed fraction is 0.70, or 70%.
With an incoming intensity of 340 W m⁻², this gives 0.70 × 340 = 238 W m⁻² absorbed. The reflected intensity is 0.30 × 340 = 102 W m⁻². Together they make the original 340 W m⁻².

The symbols I_in, I_ref and I_abs mean incoming, reflected and absorbed intensity. Intensities can be added or compared this way when all values refer to the same area. Keeping that area the same makes this an energy account.

blocks.title: Reflection and thermal emission are different
paragraphs: Reflected sunlight is part of the incoming sunlight that is sent away. A surface can also emit radiation: send out energy as electromagnetic waves because of its own temperature. This is thermal emission. At temperatures near those of Earth’s surface, much of it is infrared, a type of radiation we cannot see.

The diagram shows these as separate processes. The reflected arrow starts where sunlight arrives. The emitted infrared arrow represents energy leaving the surface because it has a temperature. That emitted power is not used in the definition of albedo.
Absorption adds energy to a surface, while thermal emission removes energy. Later we will combine them to understand when a surface warms, cools or stays at a steady temperature.
blocks.key: Albedo describes reflected incoming radiation. It does not describe the radiation a surface emits because of its temperature.

segments.title: An average can change
segments.text: Earth's albedo is often represented by one average number in a calculation, but that number summarises a changing system. Different regions have different surfaces and cloud cover. Snow, ocean, vegetation and cloud tops do not all reflect incoming sunlight in the same way. The illumination also varies with position and time. A single average is useful because it makes a planetary energy calculation manageable. It should not be mistaken for a fixed property of every square metre. When an exam asks about variations, first identify what has changed physically, rather than assuming that the number used in an earlier calculation must remain unchanged in every situation.

segments.title: Follow an ice-albedo feedback
segments.text: Consider a model in which bright ice is replaced by darker exposed water. If the new surface has a lower albedo, a smaller fraction of incoming solar radiation is reflected and a larger fraction is absorbed. Greater absorption can contribute to further warming, which can melt more ice. This is a positive feedback because the response can reinforce the original warming. The first change in the chain must be specified. Melting ice is not the same physical mechanism as a greenhouse gas absorbing infrared radiation. Both can affect an energy balance, but through different flows. Use separate arrows in a written explanation so the causal sequence remains easy to follow.

blocks.title: Different surfaces reflect different amounts
paragraphs: Fresh snow usually reflects a larger fraction of sunlight than dark water or vegetation. Cloud tops also reflect sunlight. A planet contains many kinds of surface and changing cloud cover, so its albedo is not the same everywhere.

Earth’s planetary albedo is an average for the whole planet: total sunlight reflected back towards space divided by total sunlight arriving. Places receiving more sunlight contribute more to this total than equally large places receiving very little sunlight.

As snow melts, clouds form or surface conditions change, the total reflected fraction can change. One average number is useful for describing the planet, but it does not mean every place reflects the same fraction or that the number stays fixed forever.

blocks.title: Clouds, location and time of day
paragraphs: Cloud formation changes how much sunlight is reflected before it reaches the ground. Latitude means a place’s position north or south of the equator. It is linked to differences in the angle of sunlight and in surface conditions such as snow and ice cover.

Reflection can also change during a day. Clouds move and develop, and the angle of sunlight changes. For example, water can reflect a larger fraction when sunlight arrives at a shallow angle. These changes help explain why albedo can vary with location and time.
A smaller incoming intensity does not by itself mean a higher albedo. Albedo compares the reflected amount with the incoming amount. If both fall by the same fraction, the albedo stays the same.
blocks.key: Cloud cover, surface conditions and the angle of sunlight can change the reflected fraction.

blocks.title: How melting ice can increase warming
paragraphs: Consider bright ice being replaced by darker water. If the water has a lower albedo, less of the same incoming sunlight is reflected. More is absorbed, which can warm the water and contribute to further ice melting.

This is a positive feedback. A feedback is a response that affects the process that started it; positive means it strengthens the original change, not that the change is good. Here, initial warming can lead to changes that cause more warming.

The curved black arrows in the diagram show the order of cause and effect: warming, less ice, lower albedo, more absorbed sunlight, then more warming. This is a change in sunlight reflection. A greenhouse gas changes infrared absorption and emission, which is a different process.

blocks.title: Comparing how much is absorbed
paragraphs: We can separate the effect of albedo by comparing two cases with the same incoming sunlight. With 340 W m⁻² arriving, an albedo of 0.40 leaves 60% to be absorbed: 204 W m⁻². An albedo of 0.30 leaves 70% to be absorbed: 238 W m⁻².

The absorbed intensity increases by 34 W m⁻². This is 10% of the incoming 340 W m⁻², but about 16.7% of the original absorbed 204 W m⁻². A percentage change always needs a reference amount: here it is the amount absorbed before the change.

This comparison isolates reflection by keeping other effects fixed. In the real atmosphere, clouds also absorb and emit infrared. Their full effect on temperature depends on these energy transfers as well as on reflected sunlight.

segments.title: Compare with an ideal emitter
segments.text: Every surface emits thermal radiation. An ideal black body gives a reference for how much is emitted at a particular absolute temperature. Emissivity compares the actual emitted power per unit area with that ideal value at the same temperature. A surface with emissivity zero point eight emits eighty percent of the black-body intensity at that temperature. Emissivity is dimensionless. The comparison must use equal temperatures: a hotter surface with lower emissivity can still emit more than a cooler surface with higher emissivity. This is why an exam question comparing materials often states that their temperatures are the same. That condition lets you isolate the effect of emissivity.

segments.text: The Stefan–Boltzmann expression calculates radiation emitted by a surface. It does not automatically give the net rate at which that surface loses energy. blocks.title: A reference for thermal emission
paragraphs: An ideal black body is a reference object that absorbs all radiation reaching it. It also gives the greatest thermal emission per square metre at a given temperature in this model. Real surfaces may emit less.

Emissivity compares a real surface with that reference at the same temperature. Its symbol is ε, called epsilon. An emissivity of 0.80 means the surface emits 80% of the black-body power per square metre. An emissivity of 1 means it emits the full reference amount.

Emissivity has no unit because it is a ratio of two intensities with the same units. It lies between 0 and 1 in this model. Equal temperatures matter: a hotter surface with lower emissivity can still emit more than a cooler surface with higher emissivity.

blocks.title: How temperature sets the emitted intensity
paragraphs: The Stefan–Boltzmann law gives the emitted power per square metre: I_em = εσT⁴. Here I_em is emitted intensity, ε is emissivity, and T is temperature in kelvin. The symbol σ, called sigma, is a fixed number: the Stefan–Boltzmann constant.

T⁴ means T multiplied by itself four times. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so the relationship must use that scale. For example, 300 K is about 27°C. Substituting 27 would describe 27 K instead, a very different temperature.

For ε = 0.80 and T = 300 K, the emitted intensity is about 367.4 W m⁻². An emitting surface of area A sends out a total power P_em = AI_em. Increasing the area increases total power while leaving the power per square metre unchanged.

blocks.title: Changing emissivity or temperature
paragraphs: At a fixed temperature, halving emissivity halves the emitted intensity. This is a proportional relationship: changing emissivity by a factor changes intensity by that same factor.

Temperature has a stronger effect because it is raised to the fourth power. At a fixed emissivity, doubling the kelvin temperature increases emission by 2⁴ = 16 times. Doubling a Celsius number does not double the kelvin temperature, so it does not give this result.

We can compare two surfaces by dividing their Stefan–Boltzmann expressions. The common constant σ cancels. In the ratio below, subscripts 1 and 2 simply label the first and second surface or condition. It shows separately how emissivity and temperature affect the comparison.

blocks.title: Emitting energy does not always mean cooling
paragraphs: A surface can emit radiation and absorb radiation at the same time. Its net outward transfer is the amount leaving minus the amount absorbed. Net means the result after taking both directions into account.

In the diagram, 400 W m⁻² leaves and 250 W m⁻² is absorbed. The net outward transfer is 150 W m⁻². If radiation were the only way energy could enter or leave, the surface would lose energy. If absorption equalled emission, it would have no net radiative loss even though it continued to emit.

Albedo describes reflection of incoming sunlight. Thermal emissivity describes emission at the surface’s own temperature, mainly in infrared for Earth. Wavelength is the distance between neighbouring wave peaks. Sunlight and Earth’s thermal emission involve different wavelength ranges, so thermal emissivity is not generally one minus solar albedo.
blocks.key: Emission is energy leaving. Net energy loss by radiation is emitted energy minus absorbed incoming energy, compared over the same time and area.

segments.title: A property, not a label for pollution
segments.text: A greenhouse gas interacts with some of the infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface and atmosphere. The term describes a physical property of the gas. It does not mean that every greenhouse gas is artificial or that every gas associated with pollution has the same infrared behaviour. The four gases to recognise here are water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide. All occur naturally, and human activities can alter their concentrations or the processes controlling them. Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of the atmosphere, but they are not the principal greenhouse gases in this model. Amount alone does not determine the strength of an interaction with infrared radiation.

blocks.title: What makes a gas a greenhouse gas?
paragraphs: A greenhouse gas absorbs and emits some of the infrared radiation travelling through the atmosphere. This ability affects the transfer of energy between the surface, the atmosphere and space.

Four important examples are water vapour (H₂O), carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O). Water vapour is water in its gas state. It is different from the tiny liquid droplets or ice crystals that make up clouds.

These gases occur naturally. Calling a gas a greenhouse gas describes how it interacts with radiation, not whether it is artificial or a pollutant. Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of the air but are not the main greenhouse gases here. A gas’s amount is only part of the story; its ability to absorb infrared matters too.

blocks.title: Where the gases come from
paragraphs: A source is a process that releases a gas. Water enters the air through evaporation, when liquid water becomes gas. Plants also release water vapour through their leaves; this is called transpiration.

Living things release carbon dioxide during respiration, the process that releases energy from food. Decay, or the breakdown of dead material, can also release it. Burning coal, oil or natural gas adds carbon dioxide. These fuels are called fossil fuels because they formed from ancient living material.

Methane can come from wetlands, livestock digestion, rotting waste and fuel leaks. Nitrous oxide is produced by microbes, tiny living organisms in soil and water. Fertilisers can increase its release from soils. The table gives examples of both natural sources and human contributions.

blocks.title: Why water vapour often acts as a feedback
paragraphs: Concentration means the amount of a gas compared with the amount of air. Water-vapour concentration changes as water evaporates and condenses. Condensation is the change from gas back into liquid droplets.

With water available, warmer conditions generally allow more water vapour to remain in the air. More vapour can increase infrared absorption, strengthening the initial warming. This is a positive feedback: a response that reinforces the change that started it.

Water vapour is therefore an important greenhouse gas, but that does not mean direct human releases of water vapour are the main cause of current warming. Its amount responds strongly to temperature and the water cycle, the movement of water between the surface and the atmosphere.
blocks.key: A gas can be important for the greenhouse effect even when much of the change in its amount is a response to warming.

blocks.title: The natural effect and an increased effect
paragraphs: The natural greenhouse effect happens because Earth already has an atmosphere containing greenhouse gases. The surface receives energy from sunlight and also from infrared emitted by the atmosphere. This helps explain why the surface is warmer than a simple model without that atmospheric exchange.

Human activity can increase the amounts of greenhouse gases. Burning fossil fuels, for example, moves carbon stored underground into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. The extra change in infrared transfer is called the enhanced greenhouse effect; enhanced means increased.

This is a different process from damage to the ozone layer. The ozone layer absorbs much of the Sun’s ultraviolet radiation, a shorter-wavelength form of radiation. A hole in that layer is not the explanation for increased greenhouse warming. The next unit follows infrared absorption and emission in more detail.

lessons.title: Absorption and emission
lessons.goal: Understand how molecules absorb infrared energy and how the atmosphere emits it.

segments.title: Follow radiation from the surface
segments.text: Sunlight warms the surface when it is absorbed. The surface then emits thermal radiation with a spectrum set by its temperature. At ordinary terrestrial temperatures, much of that radiation is infrared. The Sun is much hotter, so its spectrum has a shorter characteristic wavelength. Greenhouse gases interact strongly with particular parts of the infrared spectrum rather than equally with every wavelength. Some outgoing radiation passes through relatively transparent atmospheric ranges. Avoid a picture in which the atmosphere is a solid lid stopping all radiation. We need a mechanism that explains selective absorption and continued energy exchange. Start your answer with the infrared radiation emitted by the surface, then describe its interaction with molecules.

segments.title: Molecules can gain internal energy
segments.text: Molecules have internal modes of motion, including vibration and rotation, associated with allowed energy states. Absorption of a suitable infrared photon can raise a molecule to a higher allowed energy state. The photon energy must match an allowed energy difference, and the interaction must be permitted for that molecular mode. In the classical resonance picture, strong interaction occurs when the radiation frequency corresponds to an appropriate natural molecular frequency. These are complementary ways of describing the relevant frequency selectivity at this level. It is not enough to say that every molecule absorbs every infrared frequency. The molecular structure and available modes determine which interactions are possible.

bridge.text: Radiation carries energy in electromagnetic waves. Frequency is the number of wave cycles each second, measured in hertz (Hz). Wavelength is the distance between neighbouring wave peaks. A photon is a packet of radiation energy. A higher-frequency photon carries more energy: E = hf, where E is photon energy, f is frequency and h is a fixed number called the Planck constant.

blocks.title: Following energy from the surface
paragraphs: When the surface absorbs sunlight, energy is transferred to it. The surface also emits thermal radiation because it has a temperature. At temperatures near those of Earth’s surface, much of this radiation is infrared.

A spectrum is the range of wavelengths in radiation. The much hotter Sun emits strongly at shorter wavelengths, including visible light. The cooler Earth emits mainly at longer, infrared wavelengths. This helps explain why the atmosphere can let much sunlight through while absorbing some of Earth’s outgoing radiation.

Greenhouse gases absorb some infrared wavelengths more strongly than others. Some radiation passes through the atmosphere and escapes to space. In the diagram, the long upward arrow shows this escape, while the other arrows show absorption and emission by the atmosphere.

blocks.title: How a molecule absorbs a photon
paragraphs: A molecule is a group of atoms joined together. Its atoms can vibrate, moving back and forth relative to each other. Molecules can also rotate, or turn. These motions contribute to internal energy: energy stored within the matter. Molecular energy levels are the particular energy values these motions can have.

A suitable infrared photon can be absorbed, taking the molecule from a lower energy level E₁ to a higher level E₂. The photon’s energy must equal the difference between the two levels. This change between levels is called a transition. Only some transitions can interact with infrared radiation.

Resonance gives a related wave description: interaction is strong when the radiation frequency matches a suitable natural molecular motion. A mode means a particular pattern of motion. Different molecules have different modes, so they do not all absorb the same frequencies.

blocks.title: What happens after absorption?
paragraphs: A molecule in a higher energy state is called excited. It can share energy with nearby molecules through collisions. This means an absorbed photon’s energy can become spread through the gas rather than staying in one molecule.

The atmosphere also emits infrared radiation in different directions. Some travels upwards towards space, and some travels downwards towards the surface. When the surface absorbs downward infrared, it gains energy.

This is not the same as mirror reflection. Reflection redirects incoming radiation. Absorption transfers energy to matter, and emission sends radiation out from matter. There is no need for the same absorbed photon to bounce straight back along its original path.
blocks.key: The atmosphere absorbs and emits infrared. It does not behave like a mirror reflecting all outgoing radiation back down.

blocks.title: How these exchanges affect the surface
paragraphs: The surface can receive energy in two ways in this simple radiation model: sunlight from above and infrared emitted downwards by the atmosphere. It also loses energy by emitting infrared. Its temperature depends on the balance between what it absorbs and what it emits.

The atmosphere is not a solid lid. It keeps exchanging energy with the surface and with space. Some surface radiation escapes directly, and some energy reaches space after absorption and emission within the atmosphere.

These processes explain the greenhouse effect without creating energy or stopping all energy from leaving. The important change is how energy moves through the surface and atmosphere, and therefore what temperatures are needed for incoming and outgoing energy to balance.
blocks.key: Downward atmospheric infrared is an additional energy input to the surface. Energy still leaves the combined planet for space.

segments.title: Start from an equilibrium
segments.text: Imagine Earth and its atmosphere initially in a steady average state. The solar power absorbed by the combined system is balanced by the radiation leaving for space. Energy still flows continuously; equilibrium does not mean that radiation stops. Now increase the concentration of a greenhouse gas while initially holding the temperature profile and incoming sunlight fixed. The change can increase infrared absorption and alter where radiation escapes to space. Under this simplified comparison, outgoing radiation is reduced before the system has warmed. Absorbed incoming energy then exceeds outgoing energy, so the combined system gains internal energy. Starting with this before-and-after comparison makes the direction of the response clear.

blocks.title: A change in the energy balance
paragraphs: Imagine Earth and its atmosphere together, initially at a steady average temperature. They absorb solar energy at the same rate that they emit energy to space. This is an equilibrium: a state of balance. Radiation continues to arrive and leave.

Now imagine increasing the concentration of a greenhouse gas, meaning its amount relative to the air. To understand this change on its own, first keep the temperatures, incoming sunlight and reflected fraction the same.

More greenhouse gas can increase infrared absorption and change how energy reaches space. In this comparison, the outgoing power initially falls. The absorbed solar power is now greater than the outgoing power, so energy builds up in the surface and atmosphere. The bars show this change from equal input and output to input greater than output.

blocks.title: Warming restores the balance
paragraphs: When energy keeps building up, the surface and atmosphere warm. Warmer regions emit more infrared radiation. As temperatures adjust, the outgoing power can increase until it once again matches the absorbed solar power.

The new balance is warmer in this simple comparison. Equilibrium does not mean the planet has returned to its old temperature; it means energy enters and leaves at equal rates again. From the surface’s point of view, infrared emitted downwards by the atmosphere also contributes to its incoming energy.

The greenhouse effect does not create energy. It changes the absorption and emission of radiation and the temperatures needed to pass energy through the system. A warmer planet still loses energy to space. These continuing transfers are what make a steady temperature possible.
blocks.key: A warmer equilibrium still has energy leaving for space. Incoming and outgoing power balance at the new temperatures.

blocks.title: How human activity contributes
paragraphs: The natural greenhouse effect already exists because the atmosphere contains greenhouse gases. The enhanced greenhouse effect is the additional change caused by increased amounts of those gases. Enhanced means strengthened or increased.

Burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas releases carbon dioxide. Methane can also be released by livestock, waste and leaks during fuel production. These activities can increase the amount of greenhouse gas in the atmosphere.

The main effect described here concerns infrared emitted by Earth, not greenhouse gases absorbing every incoming ray of sunlight. The connection is: more gas changes infrared transfer; outgoing energy initially decreases; energy builds up; temperatures rise towards a new balance.

blocks.title: What a simple model leaves out
paragraphs: A model is a simplified description of a real system. Holding sunlight, albedo and other energy transfers fixed helps us understand the effect of changing greenhouse gases alone. Albedo is the fraction of sunlight reflected away.

Real changes can also affect water vapour, clouds and ice. These responses are called feedbacks because they affect the warming that caused them. For example, less bright ice can lower albedo, allowing more sunlight to be absorbed. That is a different starting process from increasing infrared absorption.

A simple model can explain the direction of a change without giving an exact temperature rise. The size of the rise depends on how much gas changes, how it interacts with radiation, and the other responses of the climate system.

segments.title: Draw the boundary before the equation
segments.text: We now combine earlier ideas to estimate the equilibrium temperature of a simple planet. Assume a spherical planet with a uniform model temperature, a solar constant S, a solar albedo alpha and a thermal emissivity epsilon. The model has no separate greenhouse atmosphere, no internal heating and no other energy transfers. These assumptions matter: the result is a simple radiative temperature, not automatically the temperature of Earth's real surface. At equilibrium, absorbed solar power equals emitted thermal power. Begin by drawing incoming sunlight, reflected sunlight and outgoing thermal radiation. The reflected component has not heated the planet and must be removed from the incoming energy available for absorption.

blocks.title: A simple planet at a steady temperature
paragraphs: An equilibrium temperature is a temperature at which the planet gains and loses energy at equal rates. Here we consider radiation only, so absorbed solar power equals emitted thermal power.

We use a simplified model: the planet is a sphere with the same temperature everywhere. It has no separate greenhouse atmosphere, no heat source inside it and no other energy transfers. These assumptions tell us what the calculation represents.

The diagram separates sunlight arriving, sunlight reflected away and infrared emitted by the planet. Reflected sunlight is not absorbed, so it is not an energy gain by the planet. Only the absorbed part is balanced against thermal emission.

blocks.title: Combining the areas and fractions
paragraphs: The planet catches sunlight over the circular area πR², where R is its radius. Its total incoming power is SπR². The absorbed fraction is 1 − α, so absorbed power is (1 − α)SπR².
The whole surface emits infrared. Its area is 4πR², and its emitted intensity is εσT⁴. Multiplying these gives the total emitted power. At equilibrium the two powers are equal.

Dividing both sides by the same area factor leaves (1 − α)S/4 = εσT⁴. The left side is absorbed power per square metre averaged over the planet. The right side is emitted power per square metre. The equation is an energy balance using the same area on both sides.

equations.label: At equilibrium, absorbed power equals emitted power
lines: Cancel πR², then divide by 4: (1 − α)S / 4 = εσT⁴

blocks.title: Finding the temperature
paragraphs: Suppose the global mean absorbed intensity is 240 W m⁻² and emissivity is 1. For balance, the planet must emit 240 W m⁻². The equation becomes σT⁴ = 240, where σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

Dividing by σ gives T⁴. We then take the fourth root to find T. A fourth root reverses raising a number to the fourth power: it finds the number that, multiplied by itself four times, gives the starting value. The result here is about 255 K.

The starting 240 W m⁻² was already absorbed and averaged over the planet. Reflection and the area ratio have therefore already been included. Multiplying by 1 − α or dividing by four again would describe a different, smaller energy input.

equations.label: Starting with the absorbed global mean
lines: At this temperature, σT⁴ ≈ 240 W m⁻²

blocks.title: What makes this temperature higher or lower?
paragraphs: More absorbed sunlight requires more emission for balance. With emissivity unchanged, the planet must be warmer to emit that extra power. A higher albedo reflects more sunlight, so it lowers the equilibrium temperature when the other quantities stay the same.
Lower emissivity has the opposite effect in this model. At a given temperature, a less effective emitter sends out less power. It therefore needs a higher temperature to emit the same absorbed power.

This simplified radiation temperature is not automatically Earth’s actual surface temperature. The real atmosphere absorbs and emits infrared, including down towards the surface. That extra surface energy input is missing from this model. The next lesson includes the surface and atmosphere separately.
blocks.key: A model temperature belongs to its assumptions. Adding a greenhouse atmosphere changes the surface energy balance.

checkpoint.prompt: At the same solar intensity and emissivity, why does increasing albedo lower the model’s equilibrium temperature?
checkpoint.answer: More sunlight is reflected, so less is absorbed. Less emission is then needed for balance. At unchanged emissivity, a lower temperature produces that smaller emitted power.

lessons.title: Surface–atmosphere balance
lessons.goal: Understand the energy exchanges of the surface, the atmosphere and the two together.

segments.title: One system can have several boundaries
segments.text: The surface and atmosphere exchange energy internally while the combined planet exchanges energy with space. An arrow going from atmosphere to surface enters the surface account but stays inside the combined planet. That distinction explains why surface infrared emission can exceed the sunlight absorbed by the planet without violating conservation of energy. Internal exchanges can be large while the net flow through the outer boundary remains balanced. Begin each question by choosing which object is in equilibrium. Circle either surface, atmosphere or whole system. Then count only arrows crossing that boundary. A useful diagram labels both the direction and the kind of radiation so reflected sunlight is not mistaken for atmospheric infrared.

checkpoint.text: Write an energy equation for the explicitly chosen boundary.
checkpoint.answer: Boundary: Earth’s surface. Assume only the radiative transfers in the question. 238 + Idown = 351.1. Subtract the solar contribution from the total outgoing emission. Idown = 113.1 W m⁻² (about 111 W m⁻² if the earlier “about 240” result is used).

segments.text: A longer exam question might first ask for absorbed sunlight using albedo and the factor of four, then calculate surface emission using emissivity and temperature, then request the downward atmospheric intensity. bridge.title: Choosing what we are studying
bridge.text: A system is the part of the world we choose to study. A boundary is an imaginary edge around it. A transfer from atmosphere to surface enters the surface system, but stays inside a system containing both. At equilibrium, meaning a steady energy balance, incoming and outgoing power are equal. Energy is transferred between parts; it is not created or destroyed.

blocks.title: The same transfer can be internal or incoming
paragraphs: The surface and atmosphere exchange radiation with each other. Together, they also exchange energy with space. These are different ways of looking at the same physical situation.

Infrared travelling from atmosphere to surface crosses the boundary around the surface, so it is an incoming transfer for the surface. It does not cross the outer boundary around the surface and atmosphere together. For that combined system, it is an internal transfer: energy moving between its own parts.

The dashed boundaries in the diagram show these choices. They mark what we are studying; they are not physical barriers. A transfer can therefore matter in a surface-only balance without adding any new energy to the combined planet.

blocks.title: How the surface can emit more than its absorbed sunlight
paragraphs: In a radiation-only surface model, two inputs can supply energy: absorbed sunlight and absorbed infrared from the atmosphere. Surface infrared emission is an output. At a steady temperature, the total input equals the output.

If the surface absorbs 240 W m⁻² of sunlight and emits 390 W m⁻², the other 150 W m⁻² must come from atmospheric infrared in this model. All values refer to the same surface area. The surface does not create the extra energy; it receives it from another part of the system.

Real surfaces have other transfers too. Evaporation carries energy away when liquid water becomes vapour. Convection transfers energy as warmer air moves. They are left out of this model so that we can study the radiation balance on its own.

equations.label: Surface balance with radiation only
lines: Absorbed sunlight + absorbed downward infrared = emitted infrared
I↓ means absorbed downward infrared intensity

blocks.title: An ideal atmospheric layer
paragraphs: Now consider a different example: an idealised atmospheric layer. Idealised means deliberately simplified. This layer lets sunlight through, absorbs all infrared from the surface, and emits equal amounts of infrared upwards and downwards. These are the assumptions of this example, not rules for every atmosphere.

In the diagram, the surface absorbs 240 W m⁻² of sunlight and 240 W m⁻² of downward infrared. It emits 480 W m⁻² upwards. The layer absorbs that 480, then emits 240 upwards to space and 240 downwards to the surface.

Both parts balance separately. The surface receives 480 and emits 480. The layer receives 480 and emits 480 in total. All intensities use the same reference area, so the numbers can be added directly.

equations.label: Energy balances for the illustrated ideal layer
lines: Surface: 240 sunlight + 240 downward IR = 480 emitted IR
Combined: 240 absorbed sunlight = 240 outgoing to space

blocks.key: Equal upward and downward emission is an assumption of this ideal layer. Other atmospheric models can have different transfers.

blocks.title: Why internal transfers do not add extra energy
paragraphs: In the ideal-layer example, energy can move between the surface and atmosphere while the combined planet receives 240 W m⁻² from sunlight and loses 240 W m⁻² to space. The internal exchanges can be larger than the external input without breaking conservation of energy.

When we add the surface and atmospheric balances, a transfer leaving one is the same transfer entering the other. Those internal terms cancel from the combined equation. Cancel means they no longer appear in that total, not that the radiation has stopped travelling.

This explains why surface emission alone is not the same as energy lost by the whole planet. The whole-planet loss is what crosses the outer boundary into space. Keeping these systems clear lets us understand both the warmer surface and the planet’s overall energy balance.
blocks.key: Internal exchange moves energy between the surface and atmosphere. Only transfers across the outer boundary change the combined planet’s total energy.

checkpoint.prompt: In the ideal-layer example, the surface emits 480 W m⁻² while the planet absorbs only 240 W m⁻² of sunlight. Where does the rest of the surface’s incoming energy come from?
checkpoint.answer: The surface also absorbs 240 W m⁻² of downward atmospheric infrared. Its total input is therefore 480 W m⁻². This is an internal exchange: the combined surface and atmosphere still absorb 240 W m⁻² of sunlight and emit 240 W m⁻² to space.

assessment.title: Question 1
assessment.prompt: A planet without an atmosphere has uniform equilibrium temperature 250 K, emissivity 0.80 and solar constant 1000 W m⁻². Find its albedo. Use σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴.

assessment.title: Question 2
assessment.prompt: A spherical planet intercepts solar radiation of intensity 1440 W m⁻². Its mean solar albedo is 0.25. In a steady model, all non-reflected sunlight reaches and is absorbed by the surface, which also absorbs 160 W m⁻² of atmospheric infrared. The surface loses 40 W m⁻² by non-radiative transfer. Calculate the surface infrared emission.
assessment.unit_explanation: Intensity is power per unit area.
assessment.explanation: Mean solar absorption = 1440 × 0.75/4 = 270. Surface: 270 + 160 = emission + 40, giving 390 W m⁻².
assessment.solution: Mean solar absorption = 1440 × 0.75/4 = 270. Surface: 270 + 160 = emission + 40, giving 390 W m⁻².

assessment.title: Question 3
assessment.prompt: A world gains more greenhouse gas while its incident sunlight and solar albedo remain unchanged. Describe the molecular interaction involved and explain how the world can eventually reach a warmer equilibrium without receiving more solar power.
assessment.model: Greenhouse molecules absorb suitable infrared through allowed internal energy transitions/resonant modes. They emit in different directions. At initially unchanged temperatures, altered infrared transfer reduces loss to space and causes energy gain. Warming increases emission until outgoing to space again balances the unchanged absorbed sunlight.
rubric: Selective infrared absorption connected to allowed molecular transitions or appropriate resonance.
Atmospheric emission includes both upward and downward directions.
Initial net energy gain at unchanged temperatures.
Warmer state emits enough to recover the outer energy balance.

assessment.title: Question 4
assessment.prompt: Two spherical worlds have equal solar albedo and emissivity. World A receives 16 times the solar intensity received by world B. In the same atmosphere-free uniform-temperature model, TA/TB is:
assessment.explanation: At equilibrium T⁴ is proportional to solar intensity, so TA/TB = 16^(1/4) = 2.

assessment.title: Question 5
assessment.prompt: An idealised atmospheric layer absorbs 80% of a surface’s 400 W m⁻² infrared emission and absorbs no sunlight. It is steady and emits equal infrared intensity upwards and downwards. Find its downward emitted intensity.
assessment.unit_explanation: Intensity is power per unit area.
assessment.explanation: Atmospheric absorption = 0.80 × 400 = 320 W m⁻². Its two equal outgoing intensities sum to 320, so each is 160 W m⁻².
assessment.solution: Atmospheric absorption = 0.80 × 400 = 320 W m⁻². Its two equal outgoing intensities sum to 320, so each is 160 W m⁻².

assessment.title: Question 6
assessment.prompt: Measurements show that the fraction of sunlight reflected by a region falls as bright snow is replaced by darker ground. Explain one reinforcing temperature feedback. State one other physical influence that would need to be held fixed to isolate it.
assessment.model: Lower albedo increases absorbed sunlight, tending to warm the region and melt more snow, reinforcing the original change. Hold incident intensity fixed to isolate the albedo effect; specified infrared properties or other energy transfers can also be held fixed.
rubric: Lower reflected fraction/lower albedo.
Greater absorption tends to warm and melt more snow.
The change reinforces the original perturbation.
One relevant controlled influence, such as incident sunlight, emissivity or other energy transfers.
